A published series is usually short: five to ten annual counts. Three questions recur. Is
there a monotone trend? How fast is the count changing per period? Did something change at
one point? Each has a method suited to short series, and each is wrong to answer with a
least-squares line on five points.

## A monotone trend: Mann–Kendall and Sen's slope

The Mann–Kendall test counts, over all pairs of periods, how many later values exceed
earlier ones minus how many fall below. It is distribution-free and exact for small *n*,
so it is informative where a regression's standard error would be nearly meaningless.
Sen's slope is the median of all pairwise slopes, a robust rate of change.

```{r mk}
y <- c(402, 377, 190, 268, 331)        # five years of placements
trndtst(y)
```

A monotone series is detected even at *n* = 5:

```{r mk-mono}
trndtst(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
```

One aberrant period does not create a trend:

```{r mk-outlier}
trndtst(c(100, 100, 100, 100, 900))$p_value
```

From a data frame, with a direction when one is hypothesised in advance:

```{r mk-df}
d <- data.frame(year = 2019:2023, n = y)
trndtst(d, value = "n", prd = "year")$slope
trndtst(d, value = "n", prd = "year", alt = "decreasing")$p_value
```

## The rate of change: a Poisson trend

For counts, the natural model is a Poisson log-linear trend: `log E[y] = a + b * t`, so
`exp(b)` is the **rate ratio per period**, the multiplicative change from one period to the
next. `cnttrnd()` fits it with an interval:

```{r poisson}
set.seed(3)
y <- stats::rpois(8, lambda = 200 * 0.85^(0:7))   # falling ~15% a year
fit <- cnttrnd(y)
round(fit$rateratio, 3)
```

With a varying denominator the trend is in the *rate*, via an offset:

```{r offset}
cnttrnd(c(20, 25, 30), offset = c(1000, 1500, 2500))$rateratio
```

Counts here rise while the rate per 1,000 falls, which is the finding.

## A step change

A trend test asks "is it drifting?"; a step-change test asks "did it jump once?". The best
single split point is found by maximising the between-segment difference, and its
significance is judged by permutation, which accounts for having searched over every
possible split:

```{r step}
stepchg(c(100, 104, 98, 60, 63, 58))
```

Pure noise still yields a best split, and it is not significant:

```{r step-noise}
set.seed(2)
stepchg(stats::rnorm(12))$p_value
```

## Two survey periods

Survey tables often give only two periods, each with its confidence interval. The change between
them has an interval of its own. `healchg()` gives it for every group and indicator at once.
It lists wellness indicators first, reading change as Indigenous scholars of mental health read
it, as a process of healing (Stewart 2008). Perceived mental health of adults, 2015/2018 and
2019/2022, by Statistics Canada (table 13-10-0924-01):

```{r two-periods}
h <- indiex("health")
h <- h[h$age == "Total, 18 years and over" &
         h$indicator == "Perceived mental health, very good or excellent", ]
healchg(h, "group", "indicator", "period", "estimate", "lower", "upper",
               from = "2015/2018", to = "2019/2022", qual = "quality")
```

## A pace, projected

Some counts accumulate toward a fixed number: the 94 Calls to Action of the Truth and
Reconciliation Commission, for instance. `trcprog()` takes the pace so far as a Poisson rate
with its exact interval, and gives the year all would be complete at that pace. That is a
description of the pace, not a forecast.

```{r trc-pace}
trcprog()
```

## Choosing between them

| Question | Tool | Reports |
|---|---|---|
| Is the series moving in one direction? | `trndtst()` | Mann–Kendall p-value, Sen's slope with interval |
| By what factor per period? | `cnttrnd()` | rate ratio with interval, optional offset |
| Did it change once, and when? | `stepchg()` | split point, segment means, permutation p-value |
| Year over year, with publication rounding | `yoy()` (its own vignette) | exact intervals on each change |

All of them work on the five to ten values a published table gives, and none of them
assumes the counts are large.

## The trend in a picture

`plot()` draws the counts with the fitted trend.

```{r trend-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(fit)
```


## References

Mann (1945). Nonparametric tests against trend. *Econometrica* 13(3).
Kendall (1975). *Rank Correlation Methods*. 4th ed.
Sen (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall's tau. *JASA* 63(324).
